results.title: Sequential replacement for raidz
results.body_snippet:
### Describe the feature you would like to see added to OpenZFS

I'd like to see sequential replacement (`zpool replace -s`) extended to raidz vdevs for cases when the source device is available and readable (or mostly readable).

The goal of this feature is to restore redundancy to a degraded raidz as quickly as possible. Instead of a full resilver from parity, a best-effort copy would be attempted to recover as much readable data (of in-use blocks) from the degraded disk and then a follow-up scrub would handle the repair on a subset of corrupt or missing blocks.

I'm also interested in understanding the current algorithm for sequential replacement and then exploring if [an algorithm similar to the one GNU ddrescue uses](https://www.gnu.org/software/ddrescue/manual/ddrescue_manual.html#Algorithm) would be an improvement (as measured by a reduction in the length of time required to `zpool replace -s` devices suffering occasional read timeouts).

results.title: RFC: Ablation Study — Domino vs DSpark Performance Comparison
results.body_snippet:
## Motivation

Both Domino (#685, [arXiv:2605.29707](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29707)) and DSpark add sequential/causal conditioning on top of the DFlash parallel draft backbone, but through fundamentally different mechanisms:

- **Domino**: GRU-based correction head producing additive logit deltas on suffix positions, with a dual-loss lambda curriculum that transitions from 100% backbone loss to 100% refined loss.
- **DSpark**: Low-rank factorized Markov logit-bias head (`W1 @ W2`, rank 256) + optional confidence head (per-position acceptance predictor trained with BCE).

Prior experiments have compared these methods, but never under identical conditions (same dataset, hyperparameters, verifier, and evaluation protocol). Weifan's DPace ablations (#736) and the v6 Domino experiments used different datasets and settings, making direct comparison unreliable. This RFC proposes a controlled ablation to resolve that.

Additionally, the v6 Domino experiments showed that the lambda curriculum improved the **backbone itself** by +9.1% MAL even when the GRU head was dropped at inference — meaning sequential conditioning during training can act as a regularizer that benefits the parallel ba

Hey everyone!

I recently got GR00T fine-tuning working on my DGX Spark and wanted to share my findings since I couldn't find much documentation for this specific setup. Hopefully this saves someone else a few hours of debugging.

## My Setup

- **Device**: NVIDIA DGX Spark
- **GPU**: GB10 (Grace Blackwell Superchip, sm_121)
- **CUDA**: 13.0
- **Architecture**: aarch64 (ARM)
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04

## The Problem

Out of the box, `pip install -e .[base]` doesn't work on DGX Spark. The `pyproject.toml` specifies `torch==2.5.1` which doesn't support CUDA 13.0 or the sm_121 compute capability. The flash-attention version also has no prebuilt wheel for aarch64.

## What Worked For Me

### 1. Create a fresh conda environment

```bash
conda create -n gr00t python=3.10 -y
conda activate gr00t
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
```

### 2. Install PyTorch with CUDA 13.0 support

The key is to use the `cu130` wheel index:

```bash
pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
```

You'll see a warning about sm_121 not being officially supported — I just ignored it and everything worked fine.

# Name
**0xchange** – an anonymous, low-cost, decentralized market for fiat-to-crypto exchange

# Purpose	
To create a decentralized fiat-to-crypto exchange that is secure, anonymous, and low-fee.

# Description
**How it works**
Crypto to Fiat exchanges are enabled via six main components:

- Buyers
- Sellers
- Enforcers
- Buy/Sell Board
- Multi-Signature Transactions
- District0x Staked Tokens / Governance Committee

**Buyers** are users looking to buy any cryptocurrency using fiat
**Sellers** are users looking to sell their cryptocurrency for fiat
**Enforcers** are human actors that enforce the contract (i.e. escrow holders)
**Buy/Sell Board** is the listing of buy and sell orders
**Multi-Signature Transactions** are blockchain transactions that require 2 out of 3 signatures to broadcast (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multisignature)

results.title: Desktop wait/status orchestration re-meters full cached context every 10-30s; stale 'running' subagents keep it looping (90% of weekly Pro in 15.5h)
results.body_snippet:
## Summary

Long-running Codex Desktop tasks that orchestrate subagents and background commands consume extreme weekly usage while effectively idle. The driver is that every small wait/status result triggers a model turn that re-meters the task's entire accumulated context (~140k tokens at 97–98% cached in our case), and Desktop's orchestration issues these waits on 10–30s timeouts against work that takes minutes to hours. A newly activated Pro account went from 0% to 90% of its weekly limit in ~15.5 hours this way; the account usage API reported ~290M tokens for that single day (Aug 5).

Related: #4764 (large cached contexts consuming limits). This report adds the Desktop wait/status orchestration angle plus a subagent lifecycle defect that keeps the pattern running.

## Environment

- Codex Desktop (app-server `0.147.0-alpha.1.2`), macOS 15 (Darwin 24.6.0)
- Model `gpt-5.6-sol`, reasoning `xhigh`/`max`, multi-agent + code-mode enabled
